mathprize-olympiad-2012-01.title: Vectors
mathprize-olympiad-2012-01.body:
Let $v$ be the translation vector, so $B_i=A_i+v$ for all $i$ (also for $i=0$, since $A_0=A_n$, $B_0=B_n$). Put $d_i=A_i-A_{i-1}$; going once around the closed polygon, $\sum_{i=1}^nd_i=A_n-A_0=0$.

Then $B_i-A_{i-1}=d_i+v$ and $A_i-B_{i-1}=d_i-v$. Therefore
$$\sum_{i=1}^n(A_{i-1}B_i)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n|d_i+v|^2=\sum|d_i|^2+2v\cdot\sum d_i+n|v|^2=\sum|d_i|^2+n|v|^2,$$
$$\sum_{i=1}^n(B_{i-1}A_i)^2=\sum_{i=1}^n|d_i-v|^2=\sum|d_i|^2-2v\cdot\sum d_i+n|v|^2=\sum|d_i|^2+n|v|^2.$$
The two sums are equal. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2012-02.title: Induction with perfect strips
mathprize-olympiad-2012-02.body:
Call an $m\times n$ rectangle *good* if $\lfloor mn/6\rfloor$ disjoint $2\times3$ rectangles fit in it, and *perfect* if it can be tiled exactly by $2\times3$ rectangles.

**Perfect rectangles.** If one side is even and the other is a multiple of $3$, the rectangle is perfect (tile by $2\times3$ blocks). Every integer $m\ge2$ is a sum of $2$'s and $3$'s, so an $m\times 6$ rectangle splits into $2\times6$ and $3\times6$ strips, hence is perfect.

**Induction.** We prove by strong induction on $mn$ that every $m\times n$ rectangle with $m,n\ge2$ is good; assume $m\le n$.

- If $n\ge8$: $m\times6$ is perfect (uses $m$ rectangles) and $m\times(n-6)$ is good by induction, with $n-6\ge2$. Together they give $m+\lfloor m(n-6)/6\rfloor=\lfloor mn/6\rfloor$ rectangles.
- If $m$ is even and $n\ge5$: $m\times3$ is perfect ($m/2$ rectangles) and $m\times(n-3)$ is good by induction; total $\lfloor mn/6\rfloor$.
- If $3\mid m$ and $n\ge4$: $m\times2$ is perfect ($m/3$ rectangles) and $m\times(n-2)$ is good by induction; total $\lfloor mn/6\rfloor$.

**Remaining cases** ($2\le m\le n\le7$ not covered above): $(2,2),(2,3),(2,4),(3,3),(4,4),(5,5),(5,6),(5,7),(7,7)$.
- $(2,2)$: $\lfloor4/6\rfloor=0$, nothing to place. $(2,3)$, $(3,3)$ and $(2,4)$ need $1$ rectangle, which fits. $(4,4)$ needs $2$: two $2\times3$ rectangles stacked in a $4\times3$ part.
- $(5,6)$ is perfect ($5=2+3$ as above), giving $5$ rectangles; $(5,7)$ needs $\lfloor35/6\rfloor=5$, and the $5\times6$ part already holds $5$.
- $(5,5)$ needs $4$: place a pinwheel around the centre cell $(3,3)$ (rows and columns numbered $1$ to $5$): rows $1$-$2$, columns $1$-$3$; rows $1$-$3$, columns $4$-$5$; rows $4$-$5$, columns $3$-$5$; rows $3$-$5$, columns $1$-$2$. These are disjoint.
- $(7,7)$ needs $\lfloor49/6\rfloor=8$: place four $3\times4$ blocks as a pinwheel around the centre cell $(4,4)$: rows $1$-$3$, columns $1$-$4$; rows $1$-$4$, columns $5$-$7$; rows $5$-$7$, columns $4$-$7$; rows $4$-$7$, columns $1$-$3$. They are disjoint, and each $3\times4$ block holds two $2\times3$ rectangles (standing side by side), giving $8$.

This completes the induction. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2012-03.title: Induction for (a), extremal representation for (b)
mathprize-olympiad-2012-03.body:
**(a)** We prove for every integer $k\ge0$: every nonnegative integer $n<F_{2k+3}-1$ is a sum of $k$ Fibonacci numbers (note $F_0=0$ is allowed as a term). For $k=0$ the only such $n$ is $0$ (since $F_3-1=1$), the empty sum.

Let $k\ge1$ and $0\le n<F_{2k+3}-1$. If $n=0$, use $k$ copies of $F_0$. Otherwise let $j\ge2$ satisfy $F_j\le n<F_{j+1}$. We show $n-F_j<F_{2k+1}-1$:
- If $j\ge2k+2$: $n-F_j\le n-F_{2k+2}<(F_{2k+3}-1)-F_{2k+2}=F_{2k+1}-1$.
- If $j\le2k+1$: $n-F_j<F_{j+1}-F_j=F_{j-1}\le F_{2k}\le F_{2k+1}-1$ (the last since $F_{2k-1}\ge1$).

By the induction hypothesis for $k-1$, $n-F_j$ is a sum of $k-1$ Fibonacci numbers, so $n=F_j+(n-F_j)$ is a sum of $k$. In particular every positive integer below $F_{2k+3}-1$ is $k$-summable.

**(b)** Let $N=F_{2k+3}-1>0$. Among all ways to write $N$ as a sum of Fibonacci numbers $F_{i_1}+\dots+F_{i_t}$ with $t$ minimal, choose one minimising $i_1+\dots+i_t$. We show the indices are distinct and non-consecutive:
- No index is $0$ (drop that zero term; $t$ would decrease).
- Two equal indices $j,j$: for $j=1$, replace $F_1+F_1=2=F_3$ (fewer terms); for $j\ge2$, replace $F_j+F_j=F_{j+1}+F_{j-2}$, which keeps $t$ and the total but lowers the index sum from $2j$ to $2j-1$ (a contradiction either way).
- Consecutive indices $j,j+1$ (or the pair $1,2$ with $F_1=F_2$): replace $F_j+F_{j+1}$ by $F_{j+2}$, fewer terms (for $\{1,2\}$: $1+1=2=F_3$).

Since every term is at most $N<F_{2k+3}$, all indices are at most $2k+2$. Sort the indices decreasingly: $i_1\le 2k+2$, $i_2\le i_1-2\le2k$, and in general $i_s\le 2k+4-2s$. If $t\le k$ then
$$N\le F_{2k+2}+F_{2k}+\dots+F_{2k+4-2t}\le F_{2k+2}+F_{2k}+\dots+F_4=(F_{2k+3}-F_{2k+1})+\dots+(F_5-F_3)=F_{2k+3}-F_3=F_{2k+3}-2,$$
using $F_{2s}=F_{2s+1}-F_{2s-1}$ and adding extra nonnegative terms. This contradicts $N=F_{2k+3}-1$. So the minimal number of terms is $t\ge k+1$.

A sum of $k$ Fibonacci numbers would be a representation with $k<t$ terms, impossible. So $N$ is not $k$-summable. ∎

mathprize-olympiad-2012-04.title: Dirichlet approximation
mathprize-olympiad-2012-04.body:
**Lemma (Dirichlet).** For real $x$ and positive integer $n$ there are integers $1\le a\le n$ and $b$ with $|ax-b|\le\frac1{n+1}$.

*Proof.* Split $[0,1)$ into $n+1$ intervals of length $\frac1{n+1}$. Look at the fractional parts of $x,2x,\dots,nx$. If one lies in the first or last interval, then it is within $\frac1{n+1}$ of an integer and we are done. Otherwise the $n$ fractional parts lie in the $n-1$ middle intervals, so two of them, those of $ix$ and $jx$ with $i>j$, lie in the same interval, and then $(i-j)x$ is within $\frac1{n+1}$ of an integer; take $a=i-j$. $\square$

**Main proof.** Note that by induction the hypothesis gives: $f(a\cdot t)-af(t)$ is an integer for every positive integer $a$ and rational $t$ (since $f((a)t)-f((a-1)t)-f(t)\in\mathbb Z$, and add up).

Let $N=2011!$ and $x=f(1/N)$. By the Lemma with $n=2011$ there are $1\le a\le2011$ and an integer $b$ with $|af(1/N)-b|\le\frac1{2012}$. By the remark above, $f(a/N)-af(1/N)$ is an integer, so there is an integer $p$ with
$$\left|f\!\left(\frac aN\right)-p\right|\le\frac1{2012}.$$
Since $a\le2011$ divides $N$, $q=N/a$ is a positive integer and $\frac aN=\frac1q$. Thus $\left|f\left(\frac1q\right)-p\right|\le\frac1{2012}$. ∎
